answer: HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded): In the correlation-based PCA of the twelve forms-of-capital Z indicators across the hundred-year BCE time slices (BCE 4300–500), the symbolic-capital components behave in a split fashion. On PC1 (eigenvalue 3.74, 30.3% of variance; PC1 scores rise steadily toward later periods, r(score, time) = −0.82 with BCE), hatchets/swords (+0.30), daggers (+0.27) and house size (+0.23) all carry moderate positive loadings and belong to the same positive pole as the other prestige/wealth goods — copper/gold (+0.41), pottery decoration (+0.38), depots (+0.34) — and against subsistence/utility items (sickles −0.15, axes/celts −0.24, pottery form −0.35, amber −0.24). Thus, on the dominant axis the symbolic trio is not separated from economic capital: it tracks the same general wealth-accumulation gradient as metal deposits and decorated pottery. On PC2 (eigenvalue 2.40, 19.5%; PC1+PC2 = 49.8% cumulative), however, the trio is NOT a coherent block: house size is distinctly displaced onto the second axis (+0.33), aligning with axes/celts (+0.47), amber (+0.44), monument size (+0.39), pottery form (+0.38) and monument count (+0.29), whereas daggers (+0.07) and hatchets/swords (+0.05) sit essentially at zero on PC2, remaining defined almost entirely by PC1. In other words, the two weapon categories are pure indicators of the overall capital/prestige dimension, while house size carries an additional, independent dimension of variation that co-varies with monumentality and settlement-scale goods rather than with mobile prestige objects. This pattern is stable across specifications: the deduplicated (37 unique period rows) PCA reproduces it (PC1 trio +0.28/+0.23/+0.17; PC2 house size +0.37 ≫ daggers +0.20, hatchets/swords +0.14; PC1 max loading shift 0.07), and the robustness PCA on interpolated time-series columns averaged into the same 100-year bins gives PC1 loadings r = 0.99 with the primary run and the same trio structure (PC1 +0.27/+0.22/+0.15; PC2 house size +0.31 vs daggers +0.15 and hatchets/swords +0.17, PC2 loading correlation r = 0.66). Caveat: PCA component signs are arbitrary; the positive-on-PC1 orientation reported here is purely a reporting convention (chosen so the majority of loadings sum positive), and the substantive claim is the relational pattern above, not the sign itself.

payload.hypothesis: The symbolic-capital components split across the two leading PCs: on PC1 (30.3% variance) hatchets/swords (+0.30), daggers (+0.27) and house size (+0.23) all load moderately positive together with the prestige goods copper/gold (+0.41), pottery decoration (+0.38) and depots (+0.34), and against subsistence/utility items (sickles, axes/celts, pottery form, amber), so on the dominant wealth-accumulation axis the symbolic trio is not separated from economic capital; on PC2 (19.5% variance) the trio is heterogeneous — house size (+0.33) is displaced onto the second axis with axes/celts (+0.47), amber (+0.44), monument size (+0.39) and monument count (+0.29), while daggers (+0.07) and hatchets/swords (+0.05) are near zero, remaining defined almost entirely by PC1. Weapons are thus pure indicators of the overall capital gradient, whereas house size additionally tracks an independent settlement/monumentality dimension.
payload.workflow: Parsed capital.csv with decimal commas, dropped group/color, 12 Z columns as variables over 39 100-year BCE slices (4300–500); standardized columns and ran correlation-matrix PCA (SVD). Repeated on deduplicated unique period rows (37). Robustness: time_series_data.csv *_inter columns averaged into the same 100-year BCE bins (37 slices) and re-run. Reported eigenvalues, variance shares, PC1–PC3 loadings, communalities, score–time correlations, and PC1/PC2 loading correlations between runs. PC1 sign fixed only for reporting (majority-positive sum); signs are arbitrary.
